name: Kanchenjunga & the East
tagline: Tea hills, hill shrines and Kanchenjunga
meta_description: East Nepal tours and treks: Pathibhara Devi yatra, Ilam tea gardens, Halesi Mahadev, Kanchenjunga and Makalu base camps. Prices, seasons, permits and routes.
summary: Eastern Nepal runs from the Terai wetlands of Koshi Tappu at about 75 m to Pangpema, the Kanchenjunga north base camp at 5,143 m. Most visitors come for Ilam's tea gardens, the Pathibhara Devi shrine at 3,794 m and Halesi Mahadev's caves; trekkers come for Kanchenjunga and Makalu. October–November and March–April are best.
intro: East of the Arun and Koshi rivers, Nepal narrows into a strip of hills between Sikkim, Darjeeling and Tibet. Kanchenjunga, at 8,586 m the third-highest mountain on earth, stands on the border with Sikkim, and Makalu, 8,485 m, rises above the Barun valley to the west. Below the snow lie Limbu and Rai villages, cardamom gullies, rhododendron ridges and, in Ilam district, the tea estates that started Nepal's tea industry in the 1860s. It is the least visited part of the country by foreign travellers and one of the easiest to reach from India.

For Indian families and pilgrims, the east is close. The Kakarbhitta border is about an hour from Siliguri, and Ilam's tea country begins two hours beyond it, so a 4 or 5-night trip covers Kanyam's open tea slopes, sunrise from Antu Danda at 2,328 m and the forest lake of Mai Pokhari. Pathibhara Devi, a goddess revered by Hindus and the Limbu community, has her shrine at 3,794 m above Phungling in Taplejung: a two-day drive and a 4–5 hour climb, or a short helicopter shuttle in clear morning weather.

To the west, in Khotang district, the limestone caves of Halesi Mahadev draw Shiva devotees, Buddhists who know them as Maratika, and Kirat Rai families who treat them as an ancestral site. Halesi is 9–10 hours by road from Kathmandu or about 45 minutes by helicopter. On the plains, Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve is Nepal's main winter birding site and the last home of the wild water buffalo, while the Koshi Highway climbs from Dharan through Bhedetar to the old hill bazaars of Dhankuta and Hile.

Trekking here is remote and slower than in Everest or Annapurna. The Kanchenjunga circuit takes about 22 days from Kathmandu and needs a restricted area permit, a licensed guide and at least two trekkers; Makalu Base Camp takes about 18 days through Makalu Barun National Park. Lodges are simple and trails quiet. Our packages run from a 1-day Halesi helicopter yatra to the full Kanchenjunga trek, with prices in INR and USD and transport from Bhadrapur, Biratnagar or the border included.

highlights.title: Pathibhara Devi above Phungling
highlights.text: The shrine of Pathibhara Devi sits on a ridge at 3,794 m in Taplejung, hung with bells and red cloth left by pilgrims. Most walk up from Kafle Pati in 4–5 hours before dawn for sunrise on Kanchenjunga; seniors take ponies or a helicopter shuttle from Phungling or Kanyam in clear morning weather.

highlights.title: Both base camps of Kanchenjunga
highlights.text: The Kanchenjunga circuit reaches Pangpema at 5,143 m below the north face, crosses the Sele La and Mirgin La passes, and ends at Oktang on the Yalung Glacier below the south-west face. It is a 22-day trek with restricted area permits and simple teahouses, and few other trekkers on the trail.

highlights.title: Ilam tea gardens and Antu Danda sunrise
highlights.text: Ilam's first tea estate was planted in the 1860s, and the slopes around Ilam Bazaar, Kanyam and Fikkal still produce Nepal's best-known orthodox teas. Walk the estates, taste first and second flush, visit Mai Pokhari lake at about 2,100 m and watch sunrise over the plains and Kanchenjunga from Antu Danda.

highlights.title: Halesi Mahadev cave temple
highlights.text: In the hills of Khotang, a domed limestone cave about 60 m across holds a natural Shiva lingam lit by a hole in the roof. Buddhists revere the same caves as Maratika, where Guru Rinpoche practised. Reach it in 9–10 hours by road from Kathmandu or a 45-minute helicopter flight for a same-day darshan.

highlights.title: Makalu and the Barun valley
highlights.text: The Makalu Base Camp trek climbs from rice terraces near Num at about 1,500 m over the Shipton La into the glacial Barun valley, ending at 4,870 m below Makalu's south face. It takes about 18 days from Kathmandu through Makalu Barun National Park, with basic lodges and long, steep stages.

highlights.title: Koshi Tappu birds and wild buffalo
highlights.text: Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve covers about 175 sq km of river islands, grassland and marsh on the Koshi floodplain. From November to March it holds tens of thousands of migratory ducks and waders, and it protects Nepal's last wild water buffalo. Two nights in a tented camp near the reserve suit birders and families.

getting_there: Most trips start with a flight from Kathmandu to Bhadrapur, about 50 minutes with several daily departures, for Ilam, Kanyam, Pathibhara and the Kanchenjunga trailhead. Biratnagar, about 40 minutes from Kathmandu, is the airport for Koshi Tappu, Dharan, Bhedetar and Dhankuta. Nepal Airlines has flown small aircraft from Kathmandu to Suketar airport above Phungling (Taplejung) a few days a week, about 55 minutes, but these flights carry few seats and are often cancelled. From India, Kakarbhitta faces Panitanki across the Mechi River, about an hour from Siliguri, New Jalpaiguri and Bagdogra airport; Jogbani faces Biratnagar for travellers from Bihar. By road from Kathmandu, Ilam is about 13–15 hours and Halesi 9–10 hours. Inside the region we use private cars and jeeps, as hill roads are slow and some close after monsoon rain. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Ilam, Pathibhara Devi, Halesi and Koshi Tappu need no trekking permit; Koshi Tappu charges a reserve entry fee. The Kanchenjunga trek needs a restricted area permit, about US$20 per person per week for the first four weeks, issued only through a registered agency for groups of at least two foreigners with a licensed guide, plus a Kanchenjunga Conservation Area permit of about NPR 2,000–3,000. Indian nationals also need both. The standard Makalu Base Camp route needs a Makalu Barun National Park permit, about NPR 3,000 for foreigners and NPR 1,500 for SAARC nationals, and border villages further north need a restricted area permit. Check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Ilam 5 to 16 °C, Koshi Tappu 9 to 23 °C, dry, foggy plains, clear hills
months.summary: January is cold in the hills and foggy on the plains, but the air above 1,500 m is very clear. Antu Danda and Kanyam give some of the sharpest Kanchenjunga views of the year, and Koshi Tappu is at its peak for wintering ducks, cranes and waders. Tea bushes are resting, so there is no plucking. Pathibhara can have snow and ice on the upper steps, and the high Kanchenjunga and Makalu trails are closed by snow.
months.tip: Leave the plains by 9 am in January, as Terai fog often delays morning drives and flights from Bhadrapur.

months.weather: Ilam 7 to 18 °C, Phungling 4 to 15 °C, mostly dry, cold mornings
months.summary: February warms slowly and stays dry. Maha Shivaratri falls in February or early March, when Halesi Mahadev fills with pilgrims and sadhus through the night. Koshi Tappu still holds most of its winter birds, and the tea hills are clear and quiet. Pathibhara is possible for fit pilgrims with warm clothing, though late-winter snow can close the top for a day or two. High trekking passes remain snowbound.
months.tip: Book Halesi rooms or a helicopter seat early when Shivaratri falls in February, as the village fills days ahead.

months.weather: Ilam 11 to 22 °C, Phungling 8 to 19 °C, warming, afternoon haze
months.summary: March opens the spring season. Rhododendrons flower on the ridges above Hile and on the Pathibhara trail, the first tea flush begins in Ilam late in the month, and Pathibhara is comfortable to climb again. Mornings are usually clear, with haze building on the plains by afternoon. When Shivaratri falls in early March, Halesi has its biggest crowds of the year. Trekkers start heading to Kanchenjunga and Makalu at the end of the month.
months.tip: Start the Pathibhara climb from Kafle Pati by 4 am in March to reach the shrine before the haze rises.

months.weather: Ilam 14 to 25 °C, Ghunsa −2 to 14 °C, warm days, some storms
months.summary: April is the best spring month for trekking. Rhododendron forests between Ghunsa and Tseram and on the Makalu trail below Khongma Danda are in flower, and the high passes are usually open. In the tea hills, first-flush plucking is under way. Rai communities celebrate the Ubhauli Sakela dances around the Baisakh full moon in April or May. Afternoon thunderstorms become more frequent, so mountain views are best early in the day.
months.tip: Book April Kanchenjunga departures two months ahead to allow time for the restricted area permit.

months.weather: Ilam 16 to 26 °C, Koshi Tappu 24 to 34 °C, hazy, pre-monsoon showers
months.summary: May is warm and increasingly hazy, with pre-monsoon cloud and showers building through the month. Early May is still good for Kanchenjunga and Makalu, and the upper valleys are at their warmest. The plains become hot and humid, so Koshi Tappu is no longer comfortable. Pathibhara sees steady pilgrim traffic, but Kanchenjunga views from the top grow less reliable. The Ubhauli Sakela may fall this month in Rai villages.
months.tip: Finish high treks by the third week of May, before the monsoon reaches the eastern hills.

months.weather: Ilam 18 to 26 °C, heavy rain from early June, cloud on the hills
months.summary: The monsoon reaches eastern Nepal first, usually in early June, and it is one of the wettest parts of the country. Landslides block the Mechi Highway to Phungling and the jeep roads up the Tamor and Arun valleys, and leeches appear on every forest trail. Tea gardens are green and plucking continues, so a short Ilam visit from the border is possible with flexible plans. We do not sell treks or Pathibhara road yatras this month.
months.tip: Keep June trips to Ilam and Kanyam, within three hours of the border, and allow a spare day for road delays.

months.weather: Ilam 19 to 26 °C, wettest month, frequent cloud and fog
months.summary: July is the wettest month across the eastern hills. Rivers run high, roads to Taplejung, Khotang and Sankhuwasabha close often, and flights to Bhadrapur and Biratnagar are sometimes delayed by storms. Mountain views are rare. The tea estates are lush and busy with second-flush and monsoon plucking, and the cool evenings of Bhedetar and Dhankuta attract weekend visitors from Dharan and Biratnagar. Treks to Kanchenjunga and Makalu are not practical.
months.tip: Carry an umbrella and leech socks for any July walk in the tea gardens.

months.weather: Ilam 19 to 26 °C, heavy rain continues, short clear spells late
months.summary: August stays wet, with landslides and swollen rivers on the main hill roads. Ilam and Kanyam remain the only easy trips, with green tea slopes and misty walks between showers. Koshi Tappu floods widely and its camps close or run on reduced services. Late August sometimes brings longer breaks in the rain, but most pilgrims and trekkers wait for October. Insurance with trip interruption cover is worth having for any monsoon travel.
months.tip: Check that the Mechi Highway is open before driving north of Ilam in August.

months.weather: Ilam 18 to 25 °C, Phungling 14 to 22 °C, rain easing, clearer late
months.summary: The monsoon usually eases during September, with clearer mornings towards the end of the month. Terraces turn gold, the hills are at their greenest and roads reopen as repair crews clear slides. Late September is a good time for Ilam, Halesi and the Koshi Highway hill towns, and Pathibhara pilgrim traffic picks up before Navaratri. Early September can still bring heavy showers, so check road conditions before heading to Phungling or Khotang.
months.tip: Choose late-September dates for green hills and quieter roads before the Dashain rush.

months.weather: Ilam 14 to 23 °C, Ghunsa 0 to 14 °C, Lhonak −10 to 8 °C, clear and dry
months.summary: October is the best month for almost everything in the east. Skies are clear, the Kanchenjunga and Makalu trails are open and the air is clean after the monsoon. Dashain usually falls in late September or October, and Pathibhara Devi draws its largest crowds during Navaratri, when queues at the shrine can last hours. Tihar follows in October or November. Buses and Bhadrapur flights fill with Nepalis travelling home, so book early.
months.tip: Climb Pathibhara on a weekday outside the Navaratri days if you want a shorter queue for darshan.

months.weather: Ilam 10 to 20 °C, Phungling 7 to 17 °C, Lhonak −14 to 5 °C, very clear
months.summary: November brings stable weather and the clearest views of the year. It is excellent for the Kanchenjunga circuit, Antu Danda sunrises and photography in the tea hills. Winter birds start arriving at Koshi Tappu from mid-month. Rai villages hold the Udhauli Sakela harvest dances around the Mangsir full moon in November or December. Nights above 4,000 m are very cold, and passes can get early snow late in the month.
months.tip: Bring a sleeping bag rated to about −15 °C for November nights at Lhonak and Ramche.

months.weather: Ilam 6 to 17 °C, Koshi Tappu 10 to 24 °C, dry, clear, cold nights
months.summary: December is cold, dry and quiet. Koshi Tappu is full of wintering birds, the tea hills give crisp views of Kanchenjunga, and Dhankuta's orange season is in full swing. Pathibhara is possible with warm gear, though snow can cover the top after a storm. High passes on the Kanchenjunga circuit and the Shipton La on the Makalu trail usually close after the first heavy snow. The Udhauli Sakela may fall early in the month.
months.tip: Pair December birding at Koshi Tappu with two nights in Ilam, a 5–6 hour drive east along the highway.

faqs.q: How do I reach Ilam from Siliguri?
faqs.a: Drive about an hour from Siliguri to the Panitanki–Kakarbhitta border, complete Nepal entry, then drive about 95 km and 3–3.5 hours to Ilam via Charali, Kanyam and Fikkal on the Mechi Highway. Indian citizens need a passport or voter ID. Shared jeeps and buses run from Kakarbhitta and Birtamod, but a private car is easier for families.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit East Nepal?
faqs.a: October and November are best for clear skies, treks and the Pathibhara yatra. March and April are the second season, with rhododendrons and the first tea flush. December to February suits Ilam, Antu Danda and Koshi Tappu birding but is cold higher up. June to September is monsoon, with heavy rain and road closures.

faqs.q: How much does a Pathibhara Devi yatra cost?
faqs.a: Our 6-day road yatra from Kakarbhitta or Bhadrapur starts from about ₹26,000 per person for four sharing a jeep and two rooms, with nights in Ilam and Phungling and a spare weather day. The 3-day helicopter yatra from Kanyam starts from about ₹38,000 per person, twin sharing, including a shared heli seat.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for the Kanchenjunga Base Camp trek?
faqs.a: Yes. You need a restricted area permit, about US$20 per person per week for the first four weeks, and a Kanchenjunga Conservation Area permit, about NPR 2,000–3,000. The restricted area permit is issued only through a registered agency, for at least two trekkers with a licensed guide. Indian nationals need both. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there flights to Taplejung for Pathibhara?
faqs.a: Suketar airport near Phungling has had scheduled flights from Kathmandu a few days a week, about 55 minutes in a small aircraft with 13–15 seats, but cancellations are common and services have stopped and restarted many times. Bhadrapur, with several daily flights, is the reliable choice. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for the Kanchenjunga Base Camp trek?
faqs.a: Plan about 22 days from Kathmandu to visit both the north base camp at Pangpema and Oktang on the south side, or 18–20 days for the north side only. Getting to the trailhead takes two days by flight and road, and the walk itself takes 14–16 days, including an acclimatisation day at Ghunsa.

faqs.q: Which is harder, Kanchenjunga or Makalu Base Camp?
faqs.a: Both are strenuous. Makalu is shorter, about 18 days, but climbs steeply from 500 m in the Arun valley and crosses the Shipton La early, with very basic lodges. Kanchenjunga is longer, about 22 days, reaches higher at 5,143 m and includes a three-pass day, but rises more gradually and needs restricted area permits.

faqs.q: How do I visit Halesi Mahadev from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: By road it is about 230 km and 9–10 hours via Dhulikhel, the BP Highway, Khurkot and Ghurmi, so plan at least four nights for a comfortable yatra; ours runs 5 days from ₹30,000. A helicopter flies there in about 45 minutes for a same-day darshan, from about ₹62,000 per seat with five sharing.

faqs.q: Can Indians visit East Nepal without a passport?
faqs.a: Yes, for most of the region. Indian citizens can enter at Kakarbhitta or Jogbani with a passport or voter ID and need no visa. Ilam, Pathibhara, Halesi and Koshi Tappu need no permit. The Kanchenjunga trek still requires restricted area and conservation permits through an agency. Children need a birth certificate or school ID.
